script.opening: "Since having the baby, the thumb side of my right wrist has become really painful — especially when I scoop her up or feed her. It’s a bit swollen there and sometimes it catches. It’s making looking after her hard. What’s going on?"

facts.text: Started about 4 weeks after the birth (baby, Asha, now 10 weeks). Points on camera to just below the thumb on the thumb side of the right wrist. Worse lifting her under the arms, holding her head while feeding, wringing cloths, opening jars. A bit puffy there. Sometimes a catching or creaking feeling when she moves the thumb.

facts.topic: If asked to try the test on video
facts.text: Tucks thumb into her palm, closes her fingers over it and bends the wrist towards the little finger: "Ouch, yes — that’s exactly it."
No fall onto the hand, no injury. No tingling or numbness in the fingers. Other joints fine, no morning stiffness, no swelling elsewhere. No fever, no redness spreading.
Breastfeeding. Taking nothing for the pain — worried about anything getting into her milk. No allergies. No asthma, no stomach ulcers.

First baby. Husband, Raj, back at work; her mother visits twice a week. Tired "like everyone" but coping; enjoys the baby; no low mood or anxiety beyond normal if asked. On maternity leave from her job as a primary teacher. Right-handed.

Warm, tired, practical. You are worried you’ll drop the baby. Ask: "So it will get better?" You would rather try a splint before any injection. Keen to know which painkillers are safe while breastfeeding.

ice.ideas: "I wondered if I’d damaged something lifting her."
ice.concerns: "I’m scared I’ll drop her. And I don’t want tablets that affect her through my milk."
ice.expectations: "To know what it is and something to make looking after her easier."

cues: "It’s making looking after her hard" — the impact on caring for the baby.
"I don’t want tablets that affect her" — breastfeeding and medicine safety.
"I’m tired, like everyone" — a brief check of postnatal mood and support.

checkpoints.text: Recognises DE QUERVAIN’S TENOSYNOVITIS — radial-wrist pain/swelling over the first compartment, worse with thumb/wrist movement and lifting, classically in new mothers/repetitive thumb use

Confirms clinically — a guided self-test on video, or FINKELSTEIN’S test face to face if unclear (examiner holds the thumb and deviates the wrist ulnarwards; distinguished from Eichhoff’s thumb-in-fist variant) and first-compartment tenderness, recognising imaging is not routinely needed
Distinguishes it from thumb-base (CMC) OA, scaphoid pathology, intersection syndrome and inflammatory arthritis
Manages conservatively — activity modification/baby-handling ergonomic advice, a THUMB SPICA splint, analgesia/NSAIDs (after asking whether she is breastfeeding), relative rest
Knows escalation — local corticosteroid injection if not settling, hand/orthopaedic referral (surgical release) for refractory cases
Acknowledges the impact on baby care, reassures it is treatable, and checks understanding of splinting/ergonomics
Gives practical, supportive advice tailored to a new mother, asks whether she is breastfeeding before choosing analgesia, and asks about her emotional wellbeing (NICE NG194)

Safety-nets and follows up: review if not improving, steroid injection/referral for refractory pain, ergonomic measures, and red flags (significant trauma/scaphoid concern) — conservative-first management

worked.txt: "From what you describe this sounds like de Quervain’s — the tunnel the thumb tendons run through on the thumb side of your wrist has become thickened and tight, so they catch. It’s really common in new mums because of all the lifting and scooping of the baby. I’d like to see you in person to press on the spot and do a simple test — I hold your thumb and gently tilt your wrist towards your little finger — which reproduces the pain if that’s what it is."
"It’s not dangerous and it usually settles well with the right measures — we don’t need scans."

"The mainstays are resting the thumb with a thumb splint, and changing how you lift her — scoop with your forearms rather than spreading your thumb out. I’ll show you. Painkillers help too — are you breastfeeding? That helps me pick the right ones."

"If it doesn’t settle over a few weeks, a small steroid injection into the tendon tunnel helps many people — it can occasionally thin or lighten the skin there or flare the pain for a day or two — and rarely we’d refer for a minor op to release the tendons."
"I know how hard this makes caring for her — these measures should ease it so you can manage more comfortably. How are you doing in yourself, and who’s helping you at home?"
"Come back if it’s not improving with the splint, or if it gets much worse — we’ll step up to the injection. And if you ever hurt the wrist in a fall, let me know, as that’s different."

f.learning: DE QUERVAIN’S TENOSYNOVITIS is mainly thickening and narrowing of the sheath around the first dorsal extensor compartment tendons (abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis) at the RADIAL wrist, so the tendons catch, presenting with pain and swelling over the radial styloid that is worse with thumb/wrist movement and gripping/lifting — classically in NEW MOTHERS (repeated lifting of the baby) and with repetitive thumb use. Confirm it clinically — a guided self-test on video, or FINKELSTEIN’S test face to face if unclear (the examiner holds the thumb and gently deviates the wrist towards the little finger, reproducing the radial-styloid pain — the thumb-in-fist version is Eichhoff’s test, more often positive in normal wrists) and first-compartment tenderness/swelling; imaging is not routinely needed. Distinguish it from thumb-base (first CMC joint) osteoarthritis (older patients, base-of-thumb pain), scaphoid pathology (trauma, snuffbox tenderness), intersection syndrome (more proximal) and inflammatory arthritis (other joints/systemic features). Manage conservatively first: activity modification and baby-handling/ergonomic advice (lift with the forearm rather than thumb-abducted scooping), a THUMB SPICA splint to rest the thumb/wrist, analgesia/NSAIDs (topical or oral, after asking whether she is breastfeeding — BNF), and relative rest — most settle with these. If not settling, a local corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath relieves symptoms for many (BSSH; counsel skin thinning or lightening, infection, temporary flare), and refractory cases are referred to hand/orthopaedics for surgical decompression. Reassure it is treatable and usually self-limiting with the right measures, give practical ergonomic advice tailored to childcare, ask about her emotional wellbeing (NICE NG194), and safety-net.

knowledge.guideline: [1] British Society for Surgery of the Hand (BSSH): de Quervain’s syndrome, patient information · [2] NICE NG194 Postnatal care (2021) · [3] NICE NG100 Rheumatoid arthritis in adults (2018, updated 2020)
knowledge.summary: Radial-sided wrist pain and swelling over the radial styloid, worse with thumb use and lifting, in a new mother is de Quervain’s tenosynovitis until proven otherwise. It is a clinical diagnosis. Start with a thumb-and-wrist splint, changes to how she lifts the baby and simple analgesia suited to the postnatal period. Offer a steroid injection if it does not settle, and refer for surgical release only if it persists.

points.t: Thickening and narrowing of the sheath around abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, so the tendons catch as they glide. Common after childbirth, when repeated lifting with the thumb spread apart loads these tendons, and with repetitive thumb use.

Tenderness and sometimes swelling over the radial styloid. Finkelstein’s test: the examiner holds the thumb and gently deviates the wrist towards the little finger, reproducing pain over the first compartment. Many clinicians use the Eichhoff variant (thumb held in the fist, then ulnar deviation), which is more often positive in normal wrists, so interpret it with the tenderness. Imaging is not needed for a typical case.

Base-of-thumb osteoarthritis (older, pain at the base of the thumb, grind test), scaphoid fracture (history of a fall, anatomical snuffbox tenderness), intersection syndrome (pain and crepitus a few centimetres further up the forearm), superficial radial nerve irritation (tingling over the back of the thumb), and inflammatory arthritis (several joints, early morning stiffness, swelling elsewhere) [3].

BSSH [1]: a splint that holds both the thumb and the wrist lets the tendons rest; changing how she lifts reduces the load. Lifting the baby with both hands under the body and forearms, with the thumbs alongside the fingers rather than spread, helps.

Paracetamol and ibuprofen, dose per BNF. BNF: for oral ibuprofen in breastfeeding, the amount in milk is too small to be harmful, although some manufacturers advise avoiding it. A topical NSAID is an option. Check contraindications before any NSAID.

BSSH [1]: a corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath relieves symptoms for many people. Discuss possible skin thinning or lightening, infection and a temporary flare. Surgery to release the sheath is offered only for persistent, disabling symptoms.
NICE NG194 [2]: at each postnatal contact ask about emotional wellbeing and support. Pain that stops her caring for the baby affects mood, sleep and confidence, so ask how she is managing.

model.text: Hello Mrs Sandhu, I’m Dr Patel. What can I help you with today?

Since having the baby, the thumb side of my right wrist has become really painful, especially when I scoop her up or feed her. It’s a bit swollen there and sometimes it catches. It’s making looking after her hard. What’s going on?
That sounds hard, with a new baby to look after. Let’s work out what it is and what will help. Can you show me exactly where it hurts?
model.why: Acknowledges impact; invites her to point

model.text: Here, just below the thumb on this side.
When did it start, and what makes it worse or better?
A few weeks after she was born. Lifting her, holding her while I feed her, gripping things. Resting it helps a bit.
Have you had any fall or injury to the wrist, even a small one?
No, nothing like that.
Any pins and needles or numbness in the hand? Any pain or swelling in other joints, or stiffness in the mornings that lasts a long time?
No tingling. Just this wrist.
How are you managing more generally? Sleep, mood, and help at home?
I’m tired, like everyone. I’m coping, but this wrist makes everything harder.
May I examine both wrists? I’ll compare them and do a couple of tests. Tell me if anything hurts.

There’s tenderness and some swelling right over this bony point on the thumb side. The snuffbox and the base of the thumb aren’t tender. When I hold your thumb and tip the wrist gently towards your little finger, that brings on your pain. Sensation is normal.
model.why: First-compartment tenderness, Finkelstein positive, scaphoid and CMC clear, neurology normal

model.text: Ouch, yes, that’s exactly it.
Had you any thoughts about what it might be, or any worries about it?
I wondered if I’d damaged something. I’m scared I’ll drop her. And I don’t want tablets that affect her.
Those are really sensible worries. Let me explain.

This is de Quervain’s tenosynovitis. Two tendons that move your thumb run through a tunnel on this side of the wrist. With all the lifting you do with your thumb spread out, the lining of that tunnel has thickened, so the tendons rub and catch. It’s very common in new parents. You haven’t damaged anything, and we don’t need an X-ray.
model.why: Names diagnosis, explains mechanism, no imaging needed

model.text: So it will get better?
For most people it settles with rest for the tendons and some changes to how they lift. If not, there are good next steps.

First, a splint that holds your thumb and wrist still, especially for lifting and at night. Second, how you lift her: slide both hands under her with your thumbs tucked in beside your fingers, and take her weight on your forearms. Could anyone help with the heavy lifting for a few weeks?
model.why: Thumb and wrist splint; baby-handling advice (BSSH)

model.text: I can ask for some help. I can try the new way.

For pain, paracetamol and ibuprofen are both options, and an anti-inflammatory gel on the wrist. Whether you’re breastfeeding or bottle-feeding, these are generally suitable, as only tiny amounts of ibuprofen reach breast milk. Do you have any stomach problems, asthma or kidney problems that would rule out ibuprofen?
No, none of those.

If it hasn’t eased after a few weeks of this, a steroid injection into the tendon tunnel helps many people. It can occasionally thin or lighten the skin there. If it keeps coming back despite that, a small operation to open the tunnel is possible, but few need it.
I’d rather try the splint first.
That’s a good plan.

Come back if it’s not improving in a few weeks, and we’ll talk about the injection. See us sooner if you fall on the wrist, if the hand goes numb or tingly, if the wrist becomes hot and red, or if other joints start to swell. And please tell us if you’re struggling with your mood or feel you’re not coping. Could you tell me the plan in your own words?
model.why: Review, red flags, postnatal mood, teach-back

model.text: Splint for lifting and at night, lift her with my forearms and thumbs in, paracetamol or ibuprofen and the gel. Back in a few weeks if it’s no better.
Spot on. I’ll arrange a review then.

social.t: Wrist pain limits lifting, feeding and bathing. Ask who can help, and adapt advice to her home.
Pain, tiredness and fear of dropping the baby can erode confidence and mood. Ask about emotional wellbeing (NICE NG194).

legal.h: Maternity leave and return to work
legal.t: If symptoms persist on return to work, a fit note can advise adjusted duties, and repetitive thumb work may need workplace adjustments.

professional.t: Check the BNF breastfeeding section for each medicine and share the information so she can decide.
With her agreement, the health visitor can reinforce handling advice and monitor wellbeing.

community.t: Many areas offer direct access to physiotherapy or hand therapy for splints and advice.
Community pharmacists can supply off-the-shelf thumb splints and advise on analgesia while breastfeeding.

redFlags: Fall onto the hand with snuffbox tenderness: possible scaphoid fracture
Hot, red, swollen joint or fever: septic arthritis or infection
Several joints swollen, prolonged morning stiffness: inflammatory arthritis (NG100)
ice: Idea: she has damaged something in the wrist
Concern: dropping the baby; medicines affecting the baby

playbook.diagnosis: “This is de Quervain’s tenosynovitis: the tunnel that two thumb tendons run through has become thickened and inflamed, so they catch.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Picture a rope running through a pulley. With constant lifting, the pulley swells and the rope sticks and rubs. Resting the rope and changing how you pull lets the pulley settle.”

management.reflectIce: “You worried you’d damaged it and might drop her. Nothing is torn, and the splint and new way of lifting will make holding her safer and less painful.”
management.psychosocial: Practical help with lifting where available; ask about mood; involve the health visitor if she wishes.
sharedPlan: Thumb and wrist splint, especially for lifting and at night (BSSH)
Lift with both hands and forearms, thumbs alongside the fingers
Paracetamol and ibuprofen per BNF; topical NSAID
Steroid injection if not settling; surgical release only if persistent
safetyNet: Fall onto the wrist: urgent review
Numbness, tingling, a hot red wrist, or other swollen joints

pitfalls.intro: The diagnosis is easy to spot. Marks come from a proper wrist examination, practical advice she can use with a baby, and analgesia suited to the postnatal period.

items.why: A missed fracture can go on to non-union.
items.fix: Ask about falls and examine the snuffbox.

items.fail: Requesting an X-ray or ultrasound routinely.

items.why: She cannot stop lifting her baby.
items.fix: Splint plus a safer lifting technique.

items.fail: Avoiding all analgesia because she is postnatal.
items.why: BNF: ibuprofen reaches milk in amounts too small to be harmful.
items.fix: Offer paracetamol and ibuprofen after checking contraindications.

items.fail: Missing her fear of dropping the baby.
items.why: It is the real worry behind the visit.
items.fix: Name it and show how the plan makes lifting safer.

items.fail: No mention of mood or support.
items.why: NG194 asks about emotional wellbeing at postnatal contacts.
items.fix: Ask briefly and tell her how to get help.

wordPics.pass: Recognises de Quervain’s from the history and examination, excludes scaphoid injury, advises a splint, lifting changes and suitable analgesia, and knows injection and surgery as next steps.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: shows her a safer way to lift; answers her fear about medicines with the BNF breastfeeding position without assuming how she feeds; asks about mood and support per NG194; lets her choose between splinting and injection; safety-nets for inflammatory arthritis and nerve symptoms; teach-back.

avoid.instead: “The examination tells us what this is. We don’t need an X-ray.”
avoid.why: Typical de Quervain’s is a clinical diagnosis.

avoid.instead: “A splint for lifting and nights, and here’s a way to pick her up that protects the tendons.”

legal.t: If symptoms persist on return to work, a fit note can advise adjusted duties, and repetitive thumb work may need workplace adjustments.

professional.t: Check the BNF breastfeeding section for each medicine and share the information so she can decide.
With her agreement, the health visitor can reinforce handling advice and monitor wellbeing.

community.t: Many areas offer direct access to physiotherapy or hand therapy for splints and advice.
Community pharmacists can supply off-the-shelf thumb splints and advise on analgesia while breastfeeding.

redFlags: Fall onto the hand with snuffbox tenderness: possible scaphoid fracture
Hot, red, swollen joint or fever: septic arthritis or infection
Several joints swollen, prolonged morning stiffness: inflammatory arthritis (NG100)
ice: Idea: she has damaged something in the wrist
Concern: dropping the baby; medicines affecting the baby

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is de Quervain’s tenosynovitis: the tunnel that two thumb tendons run through has become thickened and inflamed, so they catch.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Picture a rope running through a pulley. With constant lifting, the pulley swells and the rope sticks and rubs. Resting the rope and changing how you pull lets the pulley settle.”

management.reflectIce: “You worried you’d damaged it and might drop her. Nothing is torn, and the splint and new way of lifting will make holding her safer and less painful.”
management.psychosocial: Practical help with lifting where available; ask about mood; involve the health visitor if she wishes.
sharedPlan: Thumb and wrist splint, especially for lifting and at night (BSSH)
Lift with both hands and forearms, thumbs alongside the fingers
Paracetamol and ibuprofen per BNF; topical NSAID
Steroid injection if not settling; surgical release only if persistent
safetyNet: Fall onto the wrist: urgent review
Numbness, tingling, a hot red wrist, or other swollen joints

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The diagnosis is easy to spot. Marks come from a proper wrist examination, practical advice she can use with a baby, and analgesia suited to the postnatal period.

items.why: A missed fracture can go on to non-union.
items.fix: Ask about falls and examine the snuffbox.

items.fail: Requesting an X-ray or ultrasound routinely.

items.why: She cannot stop lifting her baby.
items.fix: Splint plus a safer lifting technique.

items.fail: Avoiding all analgesia because she is postnatal.
items.why: BNF: ibuprofen reaches milk in amounts too small to be harmful.
items.fix: Offer paracetamol and ibuprofen after checking contraindications.

items.fail: Missing her fear of dropping the baby.
items.why: It is the real worry behind the visit.
items.fix: Name it and show how the plan makes lifting safer.

items.fail: No mention of mood or support.
items.why: NG194 asks about emotional wellbeing at postnatal contacts.
items.fix: Ask briefly and tell her how to get help.
